source_text: Praecipit ergo non diligi mundum, neque ea quae in mundo sunt; et dicit quoniam dilectoribus saeculi Dei caritas inesse non possit: sed non ut hoc nomine dilectionis a saeculo submovendae, alterum eius quam Deum verum intellegi faciat conditorem; verum ut agnoscant fideles, nullas praesentis vitae cupiditates praeferendas esse virtutibus, ne mens eorum aut comparandis opibus, aut conquirendis voluptatibus occupata, a christianae, quae vera est, philosophiae deducatur vigore. Quoniam omne quod est in mundo, concupiscentia carnis, et concupiscentia oculorum est, et superbia vitae; quae non est ex Patre, sed ex mundo est; et mundus transit, et concupiscentia eius; qui autem facit voluntatem Dei, manet in aeternum [n37] . Mundi ergo nomine, mores hominum nihil post hanc vitam esse autumantium, diversasque mortalium tam pompas quam luxurias indicavit.
pass_a_gloss: He therefore commands that the world not be loved, nor those things which are in the world; and he says that the charity of God cannot be in the lovers of the age: but not so that by this name of love to be removed from the age he would make another than the true God understood as its founder; but so that the faithful may recognize that no desires of the present life are to be preferred to virtues, lest their mind, occupied either in gathering wealth or in hunting pleasures, be led down from the vigor of Christian philosophy, which is the true. Because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, and the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life; which is not from the Father, but is from the world; and the world passes, and its desire; but he who does the will of God remains forever. By the name of the world, therefore, he indicated the manners of humans asserting that nothing is after this life, and the diverse both pomps and luxuries of mortals.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS conditor; Blaise God as maker from nothing

pass_b_english: He therefore commands us not to love the world or the things in it, and says that God’s love cannot be present in lovers of this age. But in saying that love must be withdrawn from the world, he does not mean us to understand that its creator is someone other than the true God. Rather, he wants the faithful to recognize that no desires of the present life should be preferred to virtues. Their minds must not become so occupied with acquiring wealth or pursuing pleasures that they are drawn away from the vigor of Christian philosophy, which is the true philosophy. “For everything in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life, which is not from the Father but from the world. The world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:16–17). By the name “world,” then, he indicated the conduct of people who suppose there is nothing after this life, and the various displays and luxuries of mortals.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
